prompt: Write an essay arguing whether schools should start later in the morning.
text:
# Why Schools Should Start Later

Most teenagers are tired on school mornings, and the cause is partly biological. Around puberty, the body's internal clock shifts later. Teens begin to feel sleepy later at night and wake later in the morning. Yet many high schools start before 8:00 a.m., which forces students to wake at 6:00 or earlier. Schools should move their start times later, because the evidence shows gains in health, safety, and learning that outweigh the costs.

The first argument concerns sleep. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that teens sleep eight to ten hours each night. A teen who cannot fall asleep before 11:00 p.m. and must wake at 6:00 gets seven hours at best. Over a school week, that deficit builds up. Students then try to catch up on weekends, which further disrupts their rhythm. Moving the first bell to 8:30 or later lets students sleep closer to what their bodies need.

The second argument concerns health and safety. Sleep-deprived teens report more depression and anxiety, and they are more likely to be overweight. They are also more likely to be in car accidents. Some districts that delayed start times saw teen crash rates fall. A study in Fairfax County, Virginia, and another in Wyoming reported fewer crashes after schools started later. A school schedule should not put young drivers on the road when they are least alert.

The third argument concerns learning. Tired students struggle to pay attention, remember lessons, and manage their moods. Research from several districts links later starts to higher attendance, fewer tardies, and in some cases better grades. The effects are not always large, but they point the same way. A change that costs no instructional time and helps students focus is worth taking seriously.

Critics raise real objections. Later starts can disrupt bus routes, and districts that run multiple tiers of buses may need to spend more. Afternoon sports and jobs may run into the evening. Parents who leave for work early may struggle to supervise younger children, or teens may lose time to care for siblings. Some also argue that teens will simply stay up later, which would cancel the benefit.

These objections deserve answers, but none is decisive. Transportation costs can be real, yet some districts have offset them by reworking routes or by swapping start times, so that younger children begin earlier and teens later. Younger children are naturally early risers, so this shift suits them. Scheduling conflicts with sports can be handled with adjusted practice times and earlier dismissal for away games. On the fear that teens will stay up later, studies that tracked sleep after the change found that students slept longer, not the same amount. Bedtimes moved little, while wake times moved later.

Finally, the question is one of priorities. Schools exist to help students learn and grow. A schedule built around bus logistics and adult work hours, rather than around the students it serves, gets the order backwards. Adjusting it takes planning and some money, but the benefits last for years and reach every student.

Schools should start later. The science of adolescent sleep is clear, the benefits to health, safety, and learning are well supported, and the obstacles can be solved with careful planning. Districts that keep early start times are choosing convenience over the wellbeing of their students.
